title: Controller vs processor
tag: Classify the role each party plays in a data flow — drives liability, contracting, and notice duties.
q: You, them, or both — who answers for this data?

q-decides.q: Who decides what the data is used for (the purposes)?
q-decides.help: Art. 4(7): a controller determines the purposes and the means. Art. 4(8): a processor processes on behalf of the controller. EDPB Guidelines 07/2020 elaborate: 'essential means' (data type, retention, recipients) are always for the controller; 'non-essential means' (technical tools) can be delegated. UK note: EDPB guidance does not bind the ICO post-Brexit — the operative UK authority is the ICO's 'Controllers and processors' guidance, which broadly mirrors the essential/non-essential means analysis.

opts.label: We decide purposes jointly with another party
The customer/client decides purposes; we just process on their instructions
We process for our own purposes and for someone else's purposes

q-means.q: Do you also determine the essential means (data types, retention, recipients)?
q-means.help: Essential means are always controller-level decisions. Non-essential technical means can be delegated to a processor without changing roles. Note: because you determine the purposes, you cannot be a mere processor on any answer here — the only question is whether you are sole controller or in a joint-controllership analysis with the party deciding the essential means.

opts.label: Yes — we decide what data, how long, who gets it
We decide the essential means too; only the technical means (which servers, encryption choices) are delegated to a vendor
Another party decides the essential means (data types, retention, recipients)
opts.desc: You determine purposes; deciding essential means is itself controller-level influence (EDPB 07/2020). Two parties each exerting controller-level influence over the same processing points to joint controllership — not a controller-processor relationship.

q-on-behalf.q: Is there a written Art. 28 data processing agreement (DPA) with the party you're processing for?
q-on-behalf.help: Art. 28(3) requires a contract or other legal act binding the processor. Without it, you may still be a processor in fact, but you're missing the documentation backbone — and the controller is in breach.

opts.label: Yes — proper Art. 28 DPA in place
No DPA, or DPA missing required clauses
DPA exists, but we sometimes go beyond the controller's instructions

q-beyond.q: When you go beyond instructions, do you determine your own purposes (or essential means) for that processing?
q-beyond.help: Art. 28(10) deems a processor a controller only where it infringes the Regulation by determining the purposes and means of the processing. Merely departing from instructions — e.g. on execution details or non-essential technical means — is a breach of the Art. 28(3)(a) instruction obligation, but does not by itself flip the role.

opts.label: Yes — we use the data for our own purposes (e.g. product improvement, ML training) or set our own essential means
No — deviations are execution-level only (non-essential technical means, timing, method)

o-controller.title: You are the controller (Art. 4(7))
o-controller.summary: You determine purposes and essential means. You bear primary responsibility for compliance with all controller-specific obligations: Art. 5 principles, Art. 6 lawful basis, Art. 12–22 subject rights (EU — see UK note), Art. 30 record of processing activities (ROPA), Art. 33 breach notification, Art. 35 data protection impact assessment (DPIA), transparency duties. UK divergence: the UK regime is the UK GDPR and the Data Protection Act 2018, as amended by the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 (DUAA 2025). The Art. 22 automated-decision-making regime is restructured into Arts 22A–22D, so in the UK the subject-rights provisions are Arts 12–21 plus 22A–22D. For data subject access requests (DSARs), DUAA 2025 codifies the 'reasonable and proportionate search' standard and the stop-the-clock mechanism (the response deadline pauses while you await clarification from the requester). It also adds 'recognised legitimate interests' at the lawful-basis layer. DUAA commencement is phased by statutory instrument — verify which provisions are in force at your assessment date and check current ICO guidance.
actions: Sign Art. 28 DPAs with all your processors

Maintain a ROPA under Art. 30(1). The Art. 30(5) under-250-staff exemption applies only where processing is occasional, low-risk, and involves no Art. 9/10 data — rarely satisfied. The Commission's May 2025 GDPR simplification proposal would widen it; verify whether adopted.
Deliver Art. 13/14 notices
Be the primary respondent for subject rights requests (UK: DUAA 2025 codifies the 'reasonable and proportionate search' standard and stop-the-clock for DSARs)
Run breach analysis and 72-h notification if applicable
Run DPIA where Art. 35 thresholds met

o-joint.title: Joint controllers (Art. 26)
o-joint.summary: Art. 26: where two or more controllers jointly determine purposes and means, they are joint controllers and must agree a transparent arrangement dividing their responsibilities between them — in particular for subject rights. The essence of the arrangement must be made available to the data subject. The CJEU trio — Wirtschaftsakademie (C-210/16), Jehovan todistajat (C-25/17) and Fashion ID (C-40/17) — established that joint controllership can arise from even limited shared decision-making. IAB Europe (C-604/22) extended this to operators of industry frameworks — there, the Transparency and Consent Framework (TCF) used for ad-consent signals. EDPB Guidelines 07/2020 codify the doctrine. UK note: post-2020 CJEU judgments (including IAB Europe) and EDPB guidance are persuasive, not binding, under the UK GDPR; the pre-2021 trio is assimilated case law from which UK higher courts may now depart under the Retained EU Law (Revocation and Reform) Act 2023. The ICO's controller/processor guidance is the UK reference.
actions: Put a joint-controller arrangement in place allocating: subject-rights handling, transparency, security, breach response (Art. 26 imposes no written-form requirement, but written form is strongly recommended per EDPB)
Publish the essence of the arrangement (often a summary of the joint-controller arrangement in the privacy notice)
Subjects can exercise rights against either joint controller (Art. 26(3))
Joint and several liability for damage under Art. 82(2)–(4)
Each controller still has its own Art. 30 ROPA entry
Embedding third-party plugins / pixels = likely joint controller for the collection/transmission stage (Fashion ID (C-40/17))

If you operate an industry consent framework: in the EU you are a joint controller for the consent-recording stage (IAB Europe (C-604/22)). In the UK that ruling is not binding — the same result is likely under UK GDPR Art. 4(7) first principles, but it is not settled; check current ICO guidance

o-processor-ok.title: You are a processor (Art. 4(8)) with a valid Art. 28 DPA
o-processor-ok.summary: Your obligations: process only on documented controller instructions (Art. 28(3)(a)); confidentiality (3(b)); security (3(c) + Art. 32); use sub-processors only with controller authorization (3(d) + Art. 28(2)/(4)); assist with subject rights (3(e)) and DPIA/breach (3(f)); return or delete data after end of services (3(g)); make compliance demonstrable (3(h)). Maintain your own Art. 30(2) processor records.
actions: Maintain Art. 30(2) processor ROPA (Art. 30(5) exempts organizations under 250 staff only where processing is occasional, low-risk, and involves no Art. 9/10 data — rarely satisfied)
Notify controller without undue delay on breach awareness (Art. 33(2))
Don't process for your own purposes — that flips you to controller (Art. 28(10))
Manage sub-processor approval workflow and flow-down of Art. 28 obligations

Representative check: offering services into the Union under GDPR Art. 3(2) may require an EU Art. 27 representative; offering goods or services to, or monitoring, data subjects in the UK under UK GDPR Art. 3(2) may require a UK representative under UK GDPR Art. 27 — verify the UK requirement against DUAA 2025 commencement and current ICO guidance

o-processor-gap.title: Processor in fact, but contracting gap — controller and processor are both exposed
o-processor-gap.summary: Art. 28(3) is mandatory. Both controller and processor commit a violation by processing without a compliant Art. 28 contract. Supervisory authorities — for example Spain's AEPD — have fined both controller and processor for this gap.
actions: Sign or update the Art. 28 DPA immediately, with all Art. 28(3)(a)–(h) clauses
Document who has been doing what in the interim
Don't fix the gap retroactively in a way that hides the non-compliance — that compounds the issue

o-controller-by-default.title: Art. 28(10) — Processor that determines its own purposes and means is a controller for that processing
o-controller-by-default.summary: If the processor 'determines the purposes and means' of any processing — beyond what the controller instructed — Art. 28(10) deems them a controller for that scope. EDPB Guidelines 07/2020 expand on the test: factual control over purposes flips the role regardless of contractual labeling. Common trigger: a vendor uses customer data to train its own AI models without explicit controller instruction.
actions: Identify the out-of-scope processing precisely
Either stop the out-of-scope processing or reclassify (and accept full controller obligations including own Art. 6 basis, Art. 13/14 notice, Art. 30(1) ROPA)
Update the DPA to either narrow the scope or explicitly authorize the activity (becoming a separate controller for that purpose)
Notify the original controller if subject-facing notices need to be updated

o-instruction-breach.title: Instruction deviations — Art. 28(3)(a) breach, but you remain a processor
o-instruction-breach.summary: Processing outside the controller's documented instructions breaches the Art. 28(3)(a) instruction obligation (and your DPA), even where you are not determining your own purposes or essential means. You stay a processor, but the deviation is a compliance gap for both sides. If deviations extend to deciding purposes or essential means, Art. 28(10) reclassification applies for that scope — factual control trumps contractual labels (EDPB Guidelines 07/2020).
actions: Stop or regularise the deviations: obtain documented instructions covering the activity, or amend the DPA scope
If a legal obligation requires off-instruction processing, inform the controller of that requirement before processing unless the law prohibits it (Art. 28(3)(a))
Audit past deviations: any that involved determining purposes or essential means fall under Art. 28(10) — treat that scope as controller processing
Tighten internal change control so new processing purposes route through the controller-instruction workflow

o-multi-role.title: Mixed role — controller for some purposes, processor for others
o-multi-role.summary: Many SaaS providers hold both roles: processor for customer-uploaded data, controller for product-improvement and billing. EDPB Guidelines 07/2020 recognize this — segregate the analyses per processing activity.
actions: Map processing activities, classifying each as controller-role or processor-role
Maintain separate Art. 30(1) and 30(2) ROPA entries as applicable
Customer-facing data flows: processor with Art. 28 DPA
Own-purpose flows (analytics on customer data, ML training, billing): controller with own Art. 6 basis and Art. 13/14 notice
Be explicit in the DPA about which is which — otherwise you risk Art. 28(10) reclassification
